accroche: Relentlessly demanding clarification of an ordinary sentence is enough to make an everyday conversation collapse
contenu_vulgarise:
A friend asks: “How is your girlfriend?” The question seems harmless, almost automatic, a politeness that expects an equally brief answer. But what happens if, instead of answering, you demand to know what “how is” means exactly, and then what “your girlfriend” covers?

## The Mechanism

This is one of the experiments that the sociologist Harold Garfinkel assigned to his students in the 1960s, published in 1967 in *Studies in Ethnomethodology*. The instruction: relentlessly ask for clarification of everyday matters that go without saying, as if common sense could no longer be presumed. In one reported case, a few exchanges are enough to derail the conversation: the other person, at first annoyed, ends up asking, “What is wrong with you? Are you sick?”

Another variant asks students to go home to their parents and, for a while, behave as a polite but distant lodger would in a boarding house, instead of the family member they are. The reactions reported range from bewilderment to anger.

Garfinkel calls these tests breaching experiments. His aim is not to test anyone's patience. It is a method for making visible what ordinarily never is. A conversation, a family dinner, a waiting line hold together because everyone carries out, without thinking about it, an immense labor of shared interpretation: filling in what is implied, presuming that the other presumes the same thing as oneself. This labor is so well rehearsed that it becomes invisible; you have to break it to notice it.

## What It Shifts

Ethnomethodology (literally, the study of people's methods) overturns an intuition firmly established in the sociology of the time, that of a social order existing as an external structure, imposed on individuals once and for all. In Garfinkel, social order is never a given: it is produced continually, moment after moment, by everyone's ordinary interpretive work. A conversation does not follow preexisting rules; as it unfolds, it fabricates the self-evidence that it has followed rules.

The consequence goes beyond the university laboratory. If social order depends on this discreet, permanent labor, then it is also more fragile than it seems, and more interesting to observe in its failures than in its silent functioning, which can be seen only once it is broken.

repere.texte: In 1967, Garfinkel publishes accounts of breaching experiments carried out by his students: told to relentlessly ask for clarification of an ordinary sentence, the other person ends up asking, “What is wrong with you? Are you sick?”

carte.punch: Relentlessly demanding clarification of an ordinary sentence is enough to derail a conversation
carte.idee: Garfinkel asks his students to violate everyday self-evidences: demanding clarification of an ordinary sentence, behaving like a stranger in their own family. The reactions, from annoyance to anger, reveal the invisible interpretive work that holds all ordinary social life together.

quiz.question: Why does Garfinkel ask his students to violate self-evidences as ordinary as “How is your girlfriend?”
choix: To demonstrate that everyday politeness is a form of social manipulation
To scientifically measure each person's level of tolerance for frustration
To make visible the tacit interpretive work that ordinarily holds the exchange together without anyone noticing
To prove that most ordinary conversations in fact have no precise meaning
quiz.explication: The experiment aims neither to judge politeness, nor to measure tolerance, nor to demonstrate an absence of meaning: by breaking the shared self-evidence, it makes visible the constant interpretive work that everyone carries out without thinking to maintain the order of an ordinary interaction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the experiment of living at one's parents' home, what are the students asked to do?
choix: Behave like a polite but distant lodger, rather than like a family member
Refuse all conversation with their parents for a week
Relentlessly ask for clarification of every sentence their parents utter
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that this variant asks students to go home to their parents and, for a while, behave as a polite but distant lodger would, instead of the family member they are.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Garfinkel call the tests he assigns to his students?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that Garfinkel calls these tests breaching experiments. They serve to make visible an interpretive labor that is ordinarily invisible, not to test anyone's patience.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which intuition, firmly established in the sociology of the time, does Garfinkel's ethnomethodology overturn?
choix: The idea that the family is the basic cell of every society
The idea that language always precedes thought
The idea that social order exists as an external structure, imposed on individuals once and for all
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that ethnomethodology overturns the intuition of a social order imposed once and for all from the outside: in Garfinkel, this order is produced continually by everyone's ordinary interpretive work.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the term ethnomethodology literally mean?
choix: The comparative study of ethnic groups
The method of direct observation of crowds
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that ethnomethodology literally means the study of people's methods, that is, of the ordinary interpretive work by which everyone maintains the self-evidence of a shared social order.
